note: Original content written by an AI agent from general knowledge. Nothing was copied from a course, book, phrasebook or website. Pointing, transliteration (capitals mark the stressed syllable), register labels and gender forms have NOT been checked by a native speaker. No audio exists for any item. Nothing here was tested with learners.

registers.label: Formal
registers.text: Careful, written or official. Correct, but can sound stiff in a shop or cafe.

registers.label: Neutral
registers.text: Safe with anyone: strangers, older people, staff.

registers.label: Casual
registers.text: Relaxed everyday speech with people you chat with.

registers.label: Slang
registers.text: Friends and peers. Avoid with officials, elders and when unsure.

pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.

pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.

everyday.en: good morning (the traditional reply, 'morning of light')

pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.

pairs.situation: Asking a friend how things are
pairs.genderNote: The textbook line changes with the person you are talking to: -cha for a man, -ech for a woman. The everyday line does not change.
pairs.note: Ma nishma has no gender in it, so you can use it for anyone and avoid choosing the wrong ending. Ma shlomcha / shlomech sounds more formal or careful in a casual chat.

pairs.situation: A quick check-in with someone you know
pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.
pairs.note: Both are common openers between people who know each other.

pairs.genderNote: The textbook line changes with your own gender (margish / margisha). The everyday line does not.

pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.
pairs.note: Kacha kacha is usually said with a tilting hand.

pairs.situation: Thanking someone for a small favour
pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.
pairs.note: Plain toda is what people commonly hear for small things like a held door; toda raba is warmer and fits a bigger favour. Saying toda raba for everything can sound heavy.
pairs.confidenceReason: Frequency of use is a general impression, not measured.

textbook.en: I thank you (plural) for the help

pairs.genderNote: The textbook line changes with your own gender (modeh / modah). The everyday line does not.

pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.
pairs.note: Bevakasha is the neutral reply. Bekef is a relaxed alternative among peers.

pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.

pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.
pairs.note: Betach is the everyday word. Bevadai is correct but a little stiff in a chat.

pairs.genderNote: No gender-marked words in either line.
pairs.note: Bli lachatz means 'no pressure', used when someone says they are late or unsure.

pairs.genderNote: The textbook line changes with your own gender (maskim / maskima). Bediyuk does not.

pairs.genderNote: Both lines are gendered by your own gender: batuach (m.) / betucha (f.).
pairs.note: Enenni is literary. Lo batuach (m.) / lo betucha (f.) is how most people say it.
pairs.confidenceReason: The pointing of the feminine forms is the main doubt.

pairs.situation: Asking for a coffee at a counter

everyday.en: is it possible to get a coffee, please?

pairs.genderNote: The first line changes with your own gender (rotse / rotsa). Efshar does not.
pairs.note: Ani rotse is understood and not rude. Efshar ...? is the opener commonly heard when ordering, and it has no gender. Note that the final -h in rotseh is not pronounced.
pairs.confidenceReason: 'Commonly heard' is an impression from general knowledge; not measured.

pairs.genderNote: The textbook line changes with your own gender (ma'adif / ma'adifa). The everyday line does not.
pairs.note: Hafuch is a standard cafe order for a milky coffee (it is on many cafe menus). Asking for the drink by its menu name is quicker than describing it.

textbook.en: I want a kilo of tomatoes

textbook.en: I want to travel to Dizengoff Street

pairs.confidenceReason: Sherut payment customs not verified. Verify before relying on it.
